To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

a simple mathematical model of body weight accurately describes the observed weight variations of a large normal adult population, that the model is valid for both sexes and across a wide range of body sizes, and that a two-parameter model based on arm length and sitting stature provides an even better fit.

a simple mathematical formula accurately describes weight-for-height in normal adults and that a standardized reference model using two easily-measured body dimensions, upper arm length and sitting-height, improves the explanatory power substantially over BMI.

a simple mathematical model based on two anthropometric variables, sitting height and upper arm length, accurately describes the relationship between body weight and body dimensions in a large population of normal adults, and that the model can be readily applied to estimate the weight-for-height of individuals in both research and clinical settings.
In summary, our research is concerned with
developing a new method to assess the risk of disease associated with body weight and body size.
the search of an alternative measure to BMI for the standardization of body weight for stature.
the development of a new method for standardizing body weights for stature.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
BMI is not a valid measure of obesity and is not recommended for use in the general population.
BMI is a poor standard of weight-for-height and that a better standard is available, but that the new standard needs further testing.

body mass index (weight in kg divided by the square of height in meters) is a useful measure of body weight in adults, but it is not perfect, and it is certainly not the only way to measure body fatness.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
a new standard weight-for-height model is superior to BMI in describing the observed variation of weight with height in a normal adult population.
the model we have developed is an improvement over BMI for standardizing body size for stature in the general population.
the model we developed, based on the two measurements of sitting height and upper arm length, is a valid and reliable alternative to body mass for standardizing weight for stature.

the standard weight-for-height model is a better measure of excess adiposity than BMI.
the standard weight-for-height is a better predictor of physical dysfunction than BMI.
